section_summary: This section covers internal affairs, administrative organization, and personnel of the Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs (Gaimushō) between 1935 and 1937, with a 1945 State Department file charge slip. It contains detailed comparative data on American and Japanese diplomatic remuneration, comprehensive Foreign Office and Foreign Service personnel lists for 1935 and 1937, and internal seniority rankings. Additionally, it includes reporting on diplomatic reassignments, commercial attache expansions, the military's influence on foreign policy, Intelligence Bureau reorganization, and cultural diplomacy.

subfiles.about: Comparative analysis of remuneration, allowances, and staffing for American and Japanese diplomatic and consular personnel in Tokyo, Washington, and New York.
subfiles.summary: This concluding portion of a comparative report details the staffing and remuneration of American and Japanese diplomatic and consular posts. It notes language officers, military and naval attaches, and trade and agricultural representatives stationed in Tokyo, Kobe, and Shanghai. Detailed tables compare salaries, cost of living, rent, heat, light, representation, and family allowances for the American Embassy in Tokyo, the Japanese Embassy in Washington, the American Consulate General in Tokyo, and the Japanese Consulate General in New York.
subfiles.title: Comparative Remuneration and Allowances of American and Japanese Diplomatic and Consular Personnel

subfiles.about: Intelligence summary reporting recommendations by the Japanese Foreign Ministry's Efficiency Commission to expand commercial diplomatic and consular representation globally.
subfiles.summary: An intelligence summary extract from the 4th Marines Headquarters in Shanghai reports on a draft plan submitted on May 29, 1935, to Foreign Minister Koki Hirota by the Ministry's Efficiency Commission. The proposal recommends substantial personnel increases dedicated to commercial affairs across Japanese embassies, legations, and consulates. Specific assignments include commercial counsellors for Washington and Changchun, commercial secretaries for five countries, seven new commercial consuls, and nine vice-consuls across Asia, Europe, and the Americas.
subfiles.title: Intelligence Summary: Japan Plans to Augment Trade Envoys

subfiles.about: Letter from Professor Kenneth Colegrove thanking Dr. Stanley K. Hornbeck for reviewing and annotating his draft chapter on the Japanese Foreign Office.
subfiles.summary: Professor Kenneth Colegrove of Northwestern University writes to Dr. Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs. He expresses gratitude to Hornbeck and other State Department officers for reading his draft chapter entitled 'Organization of the Japanese Foreign Office'. He notes that the marginal annotations and corrections provided valuable aid that he will incorporate into his work.
subfiles.title: Letter from Kenneth Colegrove to Stanley K. Hornbeck regarding Manuscript on the Japanese Foreign Office

subfiles.about: Letter from Professor Kenneth Colegrove acknowledging receipt of his annotated manuscript on the Japanese Foreign Office from Maxwell M. Hamilton.
subfiles.summary: Professor Kenneth Colegrove writes to Maxwell M. Hamilton, Acting Chief of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, acknowledging receipt of the returned manuscript of his chapter on the organization of the Japanese Foreign Office. He conveys his appreciation for the department's courtesy and the valuable information provided in the marginal notes.
subfiles.title: Letter from Kenneth Colegrove to Maxwell M. Hamilton acknowledging Return of Foreign Office Manuscript

subfiles.about: Despatch transmitting official lists of personnel in the Japanese Foreign Office and Foreign Service as of July 1, 1935, and an official seniority roster as of September 1, 1935.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits comprehensive lists of officials serving in the Japanese Foreign Office and Japanese Foreign Service in response to a departmental instruction. Enclosure 1 details Tokyo ministry personnel by bureau and section as of July 1, 1935, as well as diplomatic missions and consulates worldwide, including specialized bodies such as the Investigation Committee of Cultural Enterprise in China and the Committee on Perpetual Leases. Enclosure 2 provides a complete roster of Foreign Office officials arranged by seniority and civil service rank as of September 1, 1935, covering Shinnin rank and Higher Civil Service grades one through seven.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1602: Japanese Foreign Office Officials

subfiles.about: Departmental memorandum summarizing a private conversation regarding prospective high-level shifts among Japanese diplomatic chiefs of mission.
subfiles.summary: A Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizes Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 1623 reporting a private talk between Erle R. Dickover and Saburo Kurusu. The memorandum highlights that Hachiro Arita was reluctant to accept the ambassadorship to China if the Japanese military continued to dominate diplomacy. It also notes prospective personnel movements, including Kurusu's possible posting to Belgium, Kensuke Horinouchi's expected succession as Vice Minister when Mamoru Shigemitsu returns to an ambassadorship, and the prediction that Katsuji Debuchi will eventually become Foreign Minister.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Impending Changes in the Japanese Foreign Service

subfiles.about: Despatch transmitting a memorandum of conversation between Erle R. Dickover and Saburo Kurusu regarding pending Japanese diplomatic appointments and military interference.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits a memorandum of a conversation held on January 5, 1936, between First Secretary Erle R. Dickover and Saburo Kurusu, Chief of the Bureau of Commercial Affairs. Kurusu disclosed that his own transfer to Belgium remained undecided because Ambassador Hachiro Arita was unwilling to serve in China if compelled to take direction from the Japanese military. Kurusu further indicated that Kensuke Horinouchi would succeed Mamoru Shigemitsu as Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs and expressed confidence that Katsuji Debuchi would eventually serve as Foreign Minister.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1623: Japanese Foreign Office Personnel

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet and despatch extract concerning Japanese Foreign Service appointments and plans to expand the Foreign Office Intelligence Bureau.
subfiles.summary: This file note and accompanying extract from Tokyo Despatch No. 1882 report significant administrative and personnel developments in the Japanese Foreign Service. It details the appointment of Suemasa Okamoto as Chief of the American Section and Kanzo Shiozaki as Consul General at San Francisco. Furthermore, it outlines a Foreign Office plan to expand its Intelligence Bureau by appointing press attaches abroad, establishing closer liaison with foreign publicists on Far Eastern affairs, and creating an interdepartmental body to counter foreign espionage.
subfiles.title: Document File Note and Despatch Extract on Japanese Foreign Service Appointments and Intelligence Bureau Expansion

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet referencing a State Department memorandum on the reorganization of the Commercial Affairs Bureau of the Japanese Foreign Office.
subfiles.summary: A Document File Note cross-references a memorandum dated July 15, 1936, from Roy Veatch of the State Department to the Economic Adviser (filed under 600.9415/17). The referenced memorandum discusses the administrative division of the Japanese Foreign Office's Commercial Affairs Bureau into three distinct sections.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet: Division into Three Sections of the Commercial Affairs of the Foreign Office

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet and despatch extract reporting anticipated widespread shifts and retirements among Japanese ambassadors and ministers.
subfiles.summary: A file note and extract from Tokyo Despatch No. 2090 report that internal pressure from younger diplomats and outside groups was prompting a thorough reorganization of Japanese chiefs of mission abroad. Anticipated changes included the retirement of ambassadors and ministers such as Naotake Sato, Viscount Kintomo Mushakoji, Iemasa Tokugawa, and Eisuke Fujita. The report details anticipated transfers, including Yotaro Sugimura to Paris, Shigenori Togo to Berlin, Masaaki Hotta to Rome, and Toshihiko Taketomi to Ankara, alongside plans to elevate the legation in Poland to embassy status.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet and Despatch Extract on Contemplated Shifts of Japanese Chiefs of Mission

subfiles.about: Despatch transmitting the Japanese Government Foreign Office and Foreign Service personnel list as of March 1, 1937.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits the Tokyo Embassy's English translation of the official Japanese Foreign Office and Foreign Service list as of March 1, 1937, with select subsequent updates. The extensive roster encompasses Foreign Minister Naotake Sato, Vice Minister Kensuke Horinouchi, the internal bureaus and sections, advisory bodies, and academic non-official staff ('Shokutaku') of the Investigation Committee of Cultural Enterprise in China. It provides comprehensive listings for all Japanese embassies, legations, consulates general, consulates, and vice-consulates worldwide.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2414: Japanese Foreign Service List

subfiles.about: Department of State file charge slip recording the borrowing of file 894.021 by E. Davis.
subfiles.summary: A State Department Division of Communications and Records charge slip tracks decimal file 894.021 charged to E. Davis on October 12, 1945.
subfiles.title: Charge Slip for Decimal File 894.021

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet and diplomatic despatch on the appointment of Hikotaro Ichikawa and Japanese cultural diplomacy initiatives in Finland.
subfiles.summary: A file note and Despatch No. 895 from the American Legation in Helsinki report on Japanese efforts to foster cultural ties with Finland. The despatch highlights the appointment of Hikotaro Ichikawa, formerly Secretary of Legation in Helsinki, as a division chief in the Foreign Office Bureau of International Cultural Relations. It describes Ichikawa's writings on Finland and plans for radio broadcasts and film exchanges, noting that Tokyo was actively cultivating friendship with a nation that shared historical distrust of Russia.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet and Despatch No. 895 on Japanese Cultural Diplomacy in Finland
